Why dashboards aren't enough anymore (and what AI agents unlock instead)
Tomas Hubka
Last updated: Oct 22, 2026
min read
Dashboards have been multiplying faster than they’ve been read for years. In the AI era, anyone with access to a well-structured data model can generate the view they want on the fly, which means the data team’s job isn’t building dashboards anymore. This piece looks at how the role of analysts changed.
In
the previous article
, I described how the role of a Data Analyst is changing over time and how tedious tasks that previously occupied an unhealthy amount of time in an analyst's day are now being automated. The focus of the article was on what is the essence and actual scope of Data Analysts' work, but it did not dive into detail on what can be automated and how to leverage AI beyond these routine tasks, and give it real autonomy to work as a colleague (or an intern, if you will, or want to still have enough control).
Olga Berezovsky, in her
Anticipating 2026
piece in the Data Analysis Journal, puts the shift simply:
The job becomes powering decisions for both humans and AI. Success is measured by the number of decisions you can make that are fast, causal, and safe to automate.
Benn Stancil on his
Substack
is even more direct:
"Have a drink with a person who works in technology, and they will eventually tell you how they feel about their job: They are stuck in a white collar salt mine. The majority of their day is spent slogging through grunt work that is, if not beneath them, beneath their potential. They were hired to do higher impact work; more strategic work; more valuable work."
And then, specifically about analysts:
"Analysts will say they want to be looking for strategic insights, not making yet another dashboard."
So what work is there left for analysts beyond dashboards (that everyone can now pull with ease using AI)?
The dashboard problem
A sharp observation from one of the posts I came across:
Muchas empresas no necesitan otro #dashboard, más bien necesitan aprender a leer los que ya tienen.
Y he visto este patrón muchas veces: nadie entiende qué quiere responder el negocio > se pide “un dashboard” > nadie lo lee > se pide otro.
Y es por eso que el Data Scientist tiene un papel tan importante, no se enfoca en la herramienta más bien empieza preguntando: ¿qué decisión vas a tomar con esto?
Si la respuesta que te dan es “para tenerlo visible”… ahí está tu problema.
— Yesi Days 🤓 (@silvercorp)
October 15, 2026
Translation:
Many companies don't need another dashboard; they need to learn to read the ones they already have. I've seen this pattern many times: nobody understands what the business wants to answer, someone asks for "a dashboard", nobody reads it, someone asks for another. That's why the data scientist plays such an important role: they don't start with the tool, they start by asking what decision you're going to make with this. If the answer is "to have it visible", that's your problem.
This pattern isn't new, as dashboards have been multiplying faster than they've been read for the better part of a decade. What's new is that the conditions behind it are finally changing. Until recently, dashboards were the only way for a non-analyst to get a look at the data, and if a producer wanted to see retention by acquisition channel, somebody had to build it for them. If the CFO wanted to see it by cohort revenue, somebody had to build it again. Each new ask created another dashboard that would get looked at once or twice and then quietly abandoned.
In the AI era, that bottleneck disappears, and anyone with access to a well-structured data model and a decent AI assistant can generate the view they want in minutes. Which means the role of the data team shifts from
the people who build dashboards
to
the people who decide what's worth measuring, define how it should be measured, and own the system that lets everyone else explore it safely
.
That's a much more interesting job. And it's also a much harder one.
Did dashboards ever really work?
A bold question - I know. But for as long as data teams have existed, trust has been the quiet problem underneath everything they produce. A stakehold
